Benjamites
BEN-juh-mites
n. pl.
The descendants of Benjamin, Jacob’s youngest, whom Rachel dying called Benoni, son of my sorrow, and whom his father renamed Benjamin, son of the right hand. The smallest tribe, nearly annihilated in Judges, it gave Israel her first king and the church her greatest apostle.

Biblical Definition

The Benjamites held the narrow hill country between Ephraim and Judah, with Jerusalem on their border and Gibeah, Bethel, Jericho, and Mizpeh within it. Their history swings between extremes. In Judges 19 the men of Gibeah, who were Benjamites, committed the outrage on the Levite’s concubine, and when the tribe refused to give up the offenders, all Israel went to war against them: the LORD smote Benjamin before Israel (Judges 20:35), and six hundred men survived at the rock Rimmon, so that Israel wept, There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day (Judges 21:6). From that remnant came Saul, who said of himself, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? (1 Samuel 9:21), and after him the seven hundred lefthanded slingers who could sling at an hair breadth, and Ehud the deliverer, and Mordecai, and Jeremiah of Anathoth. Benjamin stayed with Judah when the kingdom divided, and so shares the covenant line to Christ’s day. Then, at the end of the canon, the tribe that had nearly been cut off produces Saul of Tarsus, who twice names his lineage as the ground of a boast he counts loss: of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews (Philippians 3:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no BENJAMITE entry. The Hebrew Binyamin means son of the right hand; Rachel’s name for him, Benoni, means son of my sorrow (Genesis 35:18).

expand to see more

BENJAMITE, n. — A descendant of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob; one of the tribe whose lot lay between Ephraim and Judah.

Genesis 35:18 records both names: as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.

Jacob’s blessing is martial: Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey (Genesis 49:27).

The tribe was famous for lefthanded slingers and archers (Judges 20:16; 1 Chronicles 12:2), and for Ehud, a man lefthanded (Judges 3:15).

Webster 1828 does not carry the gentilic; Judges, 1 Samuel, Esther, Romans, and Philippians supply the whole biblical usage.

Key Scripture

Judges 19:16 — "And, behold, there came an old man from his work out of the field at even, which was also of mount Ephraim; and he sojourned in Gibeah: but the men of the place were Benjamites."

Judges 20:35 — "And the LORD smote Benjamin before Israel: and the children of Israel destroyed of the Benjamites that day twenty and five thousand and an hundred men: all these drew the sword."

Judges 21:6 — "And the children of Israel repented them for Benjamin their brother, and said, There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day."

1 Samuel 9:21 — "And Saul answered and said, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?"

Philippians 3:5 — "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;"

Modern Corruption

Judges 19 through 21 is the passage most often cited to prove the Old Testament barbaric, and it is in fact the book’s own indictment of what happens when every man does that which is right in his own eyes.

expand to see more

The narrative of Gibeah is told without a single word of approval for anyone in it. The Levite is a coward who puts his concubine out the door; the men of Gibeah are Sodom transplanted into Israel; the tribe defends its criminals out of clan loyalty; the assembled tribes overreact into near-extermination and then contrive a second atrocity to supply wives for the survivors. The book states its own thesis four times, and the last verse of it is the interpretation: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Judges is not modelling behaviour; it is diagnosing a nation without a king, and it is written to make the reader long for one. Reading it as though Scripture endorsed what it records is a failure of ordinary literary attention before it is a failure of theology.

The second thing to see is the trajectory from Gibeah to Tarsus. The tribe that produced the outrage produced the king who spared Agag and hunted David, and then the Pharisee who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning — and that Pharisee became the apostle who wrote Romans. Paul lists his Benjamite descent among the things he counted but dung, that I may win Christ. The tribe of the wolf, nearly cut off, is the one God used to carry the gospel to the Gentiles. That is what grace does with a lineage, and it is the reason no Christian should ever describe any family, tribe, or people as beyond hope.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Binyamin (H1144), son of the right hand; Ben Oni, son of my sorrow, was Rachel’s name for him; the gentilic is Ben-yemini (H1145).

expand to see more

Hebrew Binyamin (H1144) — Benjamin; son of the right hand, the hand of strength and favour.

Hebrew Ben Oni (H1126) — Benoni; son of my sorrow, Rachel’s dying name for him (Genesis 35:18).

Hebrew Ben-yemini (H1145) — Benjamite; literally a son of the right hand.

Hebrew itter yad yemino — shut of his right hand; the idiom for lefthanded, used of Ehud (Judges 3:15) and the slingers of Judges 20:16.

Greek Beniamin (G958) — Benjamin; Paul’s tribe (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5) and sealed in Revelation 7:8.

Usage

"The men of the place were Benjamites (Judges 19:16) — the quiet sentence before the worst chapter in Judges."

"There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day (Judges 21:6) — Israel weeping over her own judgment."

"Of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews (Philippians 3:5) — the pedigree Paul counted loss for Christ."
